19  Zone

Which region of the plot should the values stay inside? zone shades a rectangle. It is rule’s sibling: a rule draws a line and a zone shades a region, and both work the same way. A rule takes one position and spans the axis it was not given. A zone takes a pair and spans the axis it was given no pair for. Give it pairs on both axes and it is a rectangle you placed.

Spanning the axis it was given nothing for is what this mark shares with rule, and it sets the two apart from the other marks. A rule’s line and a zone’s rectangle both run from one edge of the panel, the region inside the axes where the data is drawn, to the other.

19.1 A band across the panel

Were sales inside the target each year? You could print the two target numbers in the caption. A reader would then have to check one year at a time. A band shaded behind the line shows every year together. The quarterly table holds one sales figure for each year, and target_band holds the two edges of a target band:

quarterly: first 5 of 19 rows
year sales
2005 95
2006 104
2007 118
2008 112
2009 88
target_band: its one row
lower upper
150 175

Here are the sales with the target band behind them, 150 to 175, across every year the table holds:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A target band, 150 to 175")
(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A target band, 150 to 175"))
data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) + style(color = "seagreen") + line +
  point + y_label("Sales") + title("A target band, 150 to 175")
plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)), style({ color: "seagreen" }),
  line, point, y_label("Sales"), title("A target band, 150 to 175"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper, and also a line and points.”

bounds(lower, upper) names the two columns holding the bottom and top, in that order. The names are the table’s own, and any two columns will do: for columns called low and high, write bounds(low, high). Nothing names a left or a right, so the zone takes those from the panel and runs edge to edge.

quarterly is named once, at the start. A data() written later gives its table only to the mark right after it, so target_band is the zone’s table, and the line and the points read quarterly, the plot’s table (Data).

The zone is written before the line and the points. The marks are drawn in the order they are written, and a highlight belongs behind what it highlights (Which orders matter). A zone is pale by default, so a zone written last only tints the line and the points inside the band. A solid zone shows what the order does. Both plots below set the zone’s opacity to 1 and color the line and points black. The zone is written first on the left and last on the right:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
   data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) +
     style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 1) +
   line + style(color = "black") + point + style(color = "black") +
   y_label("Sales") + title("Zone first: every point shows")) |
  (data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
     line + style(color = "black") + point + style(color = "black") +
     data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) +
       style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 1) +
     y_label("Sales") + title("Zone last: four points hidden"))
((data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
   data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) +
     style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 1) +
   line + style(color = "black") + point + style(color = "black") +
   y_label("Sales") + title("Zone first: every point shows")) |
  (data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
     line + style(color = "black") + point + style(color = "black") +
     data(target_band) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) +
       style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 1) +
     y_label("Sales") + title("Zone last: four points hidden")))
(data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(target_band) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) + style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 1) +
  line + style(color = "black") + point + style(color = "black") +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Zone first: every point shows")) |
  (data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + line +
  style(color = "black") + point + style(color = "black") +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(:lower, :upper) +
  style(color = "seagreen", opacity = 1) + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Zone last: four points hidden"))
beside(plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(target_band),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "seagreen", opacity: 1 }), line,
  style({ color: "black" }), point, style({ color: "black" }),
  y_label("Sales"), title("Zone first: every point shows")),
  plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), line,
  style({ color: "black" }), point, style({ color: "black" }),
  data(target_band), layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  style({ color: "seagreen", opacity: 1 }), y_label("Sales"),
  title("Zone last: four points hidden")))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper, with opacity 1, and also a line and points, beside the same with the zone written after the points.”

On the left, all nineteen points show, and the line runs through the band in plain view. On the right, the zone covers the four years inside the band, 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2022. Their points are gone, and the line disappears wherever it crosses the band. A highlight written first stays behind the data at any opacity.

19.2 A band up the panel

Some highlights are periods of time rather than ranges of value. The years of a recession are one such period, when the question is how sales changed during them. Name the other pair, start and end, and the rectangle runs up the panel instead of across it. bounds() takes its first pair, lower and upper, by position, and its second pair, start and end, only by name. Two columns without names fill the first pair, whatever the columns are called, so bounds(start, end) without names bounds y, and gog gives no message. In start = start, the first start is the side, and the second is the column in recessions. The recessions table holds the two slumps, each with a start year and an end year:

recessions: all 2 rows
start end slump
2007.9 2009.5 Financial crisis
2020.0 2020.9 Pandemic
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "indianred") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Two slumps, from one table")
(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(color = "indianred") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Two slumps, from one table"))
data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(recessions) +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "indianred") + line + point + y_label("Sales") +
  title("Two slumps, from one table")
plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(recessions),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "indianred" }), line, point, y_label("Sales"),
  title("Two slumps, from one table"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end, and also a line and points.”

Two shaded periods, and only one zone in the sentence. One row is one rectangle, so a two-row table draws two bands. The same property lets one rule table draw three thresholds. Add a row and a third band appears with no change to the sentence.

Look at where the red reaches: the top and bottom of the panel exactly. That is the thing a ribbon cannot do. A ribbon is bounded by its data, so it stops at whatever numbers you give it. Any number big enough to reach the top would widen the axis to include it, so the highlight would change the plot it was meant to mark.

A ribbon does not take the start/end pair either. The score_band table, from A pre-computed band in the ribbon chapter, holds one row per raw score on a test, with the two ends of a 95% band in lower and upper:

score_band: first 5 of 21 rows
score expected lower upper
0 0 0.0000000 0.000000
1 1 0.0000000 2.960000
2 2 0.0000000 4.697929
3 3 0.0000000 6.211178
4 4 0.4027613 7.597239

The ribbon draws the band from the first pair, bounds(lower, upper):

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
  style(color = "indianred") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed measurement band")
(data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + x(col.score) +
  style(color = "indianred") +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed measurement band"))
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) + x(:score) +
  style(color = "indianred") + y_label("Expected true score") +
  x_label("Raw score") + title("A pre-computed measurement band")
plot(data(score_band), layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  x(col.score), style({ color: "indianred" }),
  y_label("Expected true score"), x_label("Raw score"),
  title("A pre-computed measurement band"))

“Given the score band: a ribbon from lower to upper, x is score.”

The ribbon runs along x, the raw scores. The band is widest at a raw score of 10, from 5.5 to 14.5, and it closes at 0 and at 20. At each score the ribbon has a bottom and a top, and nothing else: it has no left or right side for start and end to set. Give the same two columns to the second pair, and gog refuses the sentence:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(start = lower, end = upper) + x(score) +
  style(color = "indianred")
(data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(start=col.lower, end=col.upper) + x(col.score) +
  style(color = "indianred"))
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(start = :lower, var"end" = :upper) +
  x(:score) + style(color = "indianred")
plot(data(score_band),
  layer(ribbon, bounds({ start: col.lower, end: col.upper })),
  x(col.score), style({ color: "indianred" }))
Error:
! gog: `bounds(start, end)` bounds a rectangle along the domain axis, and a `ribbon` has no extent there — it spans the measure axis at each position. Keep `bounds(lower, upper)`, or use `zone` to shade a rectangle.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message names two fixes: keep bounds(lower, upper), as the ribbon above does, or use zone when a rectangle is what you want, as for the recessions.

The pair is called start/end rather than left/right on purpose. Left and right are facts about a screen. This grammar takes orientation from the bindings, so the same words still apply when x is drawn as an angle, in polar coordinates.

19.3 Both pairs: a rectangle

Sometimes the region to highlight is bounded on both axes: these five years, this range of sales, and nothing outside either. That is a rectangle closed on all four sides, rather than a band across the panel. Name all four and neither axis comes from the panel:

sales_box: its one row
start end lower upper
2015 2019 145 190
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(lower, upper, start = start, end = end) +
    style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A rectangle over five years of sales")
(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper, start=col.start, end=col.end) +
    style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A rectangle over five years of sales"))
data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(sales_box) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper, start = :start, var"end" = :end) +
  style(color = "goldenrod", opacity = 0.3) + line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A rectangle over five years of sales")
plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(sales_box),
  layer(zone,
  bounds(col.lower, col.upper, { start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  style({ color: "goldenrod", opacity: 0.3 }), line, point,
  y_label("Sales"), title("A rectangle over five years of sales"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a sales box zone from lower to upper and from start to end, and also a line and points.”

The four arguments come in two pairs. The first pair, lower and upper, gives the bottom and the top, as it did for the target band, and it can be written by position. The second pair, start and end, gives the left and right sides, as it did for the recessions, and it is always written by name, even when all four arguments are given. Four columns written by position are refused, and the message shows the spelling that works:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(lower, upper, start, end) +
  line
(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(sales_box) + zone * bounds(col.lower, col.upper, col.start, col.end) +
  line)
data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(sales_box) +
  zone * bounds(:lower, :upper, :start, :end) + line
plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(sales_box),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.lower, col.upper, col.start, col.end)), line)
Error:
! gog: `bounds()` takes at most two columns by position, `lower` and `upper`. The other pair is written by name: `bounds(lo, hi, start = a, end = b)`.

The first pair always bounds the axis that carries the measured numbers, here y. On a plot measured along x, the same first pair gives the left and right sides, as the schedule in the next section shows.

So one atom covers the three shapes a highlight needs: a band across the panel, a band up it, and a rectangle bounded on both axes. The pairs you name decide which one you get, so there is no separate atom for each.

19.4 Which axis the pair bounds: a schedule

A project schedule lists each task with the week it begins and the week it finishes. Its usual picture is one bar per task, one above the other, each running across the page from its first week to its last. Drawing it means putting the measurement on x, and putting a category on y does that.

The first two arguments of bounds() bound the measure axis, the axis that carries the measured numbers. In the sales plots they were the columns lower and upper. Every plot to this point has measured along y, so every such band has run across the panel. Now put a category on y instead. The measure moves to x, and the first two arguments of bounds() bound it there.

The schedule table holds five tasks, each with the week it begins, begin, and the week it finishes, finish:

schedule: all 5 rows
task begin finish
Plan 0 2
Design 2 5
Build 4 10
Test 9 12
Launch 12 13
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(schedule) + zone * bounds(begin, finish) + y(task) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.2) +
  x_label("Week") + y_label("Task") + title("A schedule, one bar per task")
(data(schedule) + zone * bounds(col.begin, col.finish) + y(col.task) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.2) +
  x_label("Week") + y_label("Task") + title("A schedule, one bar per task"))
data(schedule) + zone * bounds(:begin, :finish) + y(:task) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.2) + x_label("Week") + y_label("Task") +
  title("A schedule, one bar per task")
plot(data(schedule), layer(zone, bounds(col.begin, col.finish)),
  y(col.task), style({ opacity: 1, gap: 0.2 }), x_label("Week"),
  y_label("Task"), title("A schedule, one bar per task"))

“Given the schedule: zones from begin to finish, y is task.”

Read it from the top. Plan takes the first two weeks, and Launch takes the last one, from week 12 to week 13. Build is the longest task, from week 4 to week 10. It begins before Design finishes in week 5, and Test begins in week 9, before Build finishes.

Each bar is a zone, drawn from one row of the table, and its height is the task’s slot. Here the zones are the data rather than a highlight behind it, so opacity = 1 draws them solid. A zone fills its whole slot unless told otherwise, and gap = 0.2 leaves a fifth of each task’s slot empty, so the bars are apart from each other as a bar chart’s are (The gap beside each bar).

The schedule names only the first pair. A second pair can still be given on a categorical axis, and its numbers are then positions among the slots rather than values of a column. What it refuses shows what happens when the units are wrong.

The plot works because the first two arguments of bounds() name the measure axis, not the bottom and the top of a screen. gog never asks which way the screen runs; it asks what each axis carries. Here y carries a category, so y is divided into slots, one part of the axis for each category. The measurement can only go on x. This is the rule bar already follows: one categorical position, one measured position, and their types decide the orientation. It is why there is nothing like ggplot2’s coord_flip() to write.

19.5 Coloring the zones

The two recession bands in the sales plot are both the same red, which leaves them unnamed. Color each by its name and the legend says which is which, with no note on the plot. Each row is its own rectangle, so color maps per row. recessions carries a name for each slump:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) + color(slump) +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Named, and keyed by the legend")
(data(quarterly) + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start=col.start, end=col.end) + color(col.slump) +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("Named, and keyed by the legend"))
data(quarterly) + x(:year) + y(:sales) + data(recessions) +
  zone * bounds(start = :start, var"end" = :end) + color(:slump) + line +
  point + y_label("Sales") + title("Named, and keyed by the legend")
plot(data(quarterly), x(col.year), y(col.sales), data(recessions),
  layer(zone, bounds({ start: col.start, end: col.end })),
  color(col.slump), line, point, y_label("Sales"),
  title("Named, and keyed by the legend"))

“Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end colored by slump, and also a line and points.”

The financial crisis is the pale blue band and the pandemic the pale orange one. The legend names both, so the plot needs no note.

19.6 Rectangles that are the data

The schedule’s bars were the data, but every other zone so far has been a highlight: a rectangle behind a line, saying where to look. The schedule’s sentence, zone * bounds(begin, finish) + y(task), shows the general form: a pair on the measure axis and a category on the other position. Each category’s rectangle then runs from one number to another, with no other mark behind it. The candlestick below is drawn this way.

19.6.1 The candlestick

A candlestick shows how a price moved in each trading session. Each session has four numbers: the price at the start (open) and the end (close), and the highest (high) and lowest (low) prices in between. gog needs no new channels for them, because a rectangle’s sides read the pair a ribbon and an interval already read. Low to high is a whisker, and open to close is a rectangle, so the chart is two layers over one table.

That table needs one row for each session, with the four prices as columns and a column that names the session. Most price data already has this shape, and so does the book’s sessions table. It names each session twice: by its number, 01 to 14, in session, and by its date in day:

sessions: first 5 of 14 rows
session day open close high low
01 2026-03-02 100.39 100.45 100.66 99.98
02 2026-03-03 99.41 99.72 99.93 98.66
03 2026-03-04 101.02 103.11 104.19 100.53
04 2026-03-05 102.09 102.01 102.98 101.60
05 2026-03-06 105.03 104.85 105.71 103.86

A candlestick’s color shows the direction the price moved in each session, up or down. That color needs one more column, which you add before the plot. A channel takes a column name and nothing else, so color() cannot compare close with open itself (Data). You choose the column’s name, and its two values can be any two words. The book calls the column dir, short for direction. Its value is up when close is at or above open, and down otherwise. The candles table is sessions with dir added. Each language adds it in two steps:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
candles <- sessions
candles$dir <- ifelse(candles$close >= candles$open, "up", "down")
candles = sessions.copy()
candles["dir"] = ["up" if c >= o else "down"
                  for o, c in zip(candles["open"], candles["close"])]
candles = copy(sessions)
candles["dir"] = ifelse.(candles["close"] .>= candles["open"], "up", "down")
const candles = { ...sessions };
candles.dir = candles.close.map((c, i) => (c >= candles.open[i] ? "up" : "down"));
candles: first 5 of 14 rows
session day open close high low dir
01 2026-03-02 100.39 100.45 100.66 99.98 up
02 2026-03-03 99.41 99.72 99.93 98.66 up
03 2026-03-04 101.02 103.11 104.19 100.53 up
04 2026-03-05 102.09 102.01 102.98 101.60 down
05 2026-03-06 105.03 104.85 105.71 103.86 down

The body is the rectangle from open to close, and bounds(open, close) draws it from the lower of the two to the higher. Each body is drawn with style(gap = 0.4), so it takes 0.6 of its session’s slot:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(candles) + x(session) +
  interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) +
  zone * bounds(open, close) +
    color(dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette(c(up = "seagreen", down = "indianred")) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions")
(data(candles) + x(col.session) +
  interval * bounds(col.low, col.high) + color(col.dir) +
  zone * bounds(col.open, col.close) +
    color(col.dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette({"up": "seagreen", "down": "indianred"}) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions"))
data(candles) + x(:session) + interval * bounds(:low, :high) +
  color(:dir) + zone * bounds(:open, :close) + color(:dir) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette(["up" => "seagreen", "down" => "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions")
plot(data(candles), x(col.session),
  layer(interval, bounds(col.low, col.high)), color(col.dir),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.open, col.close)), color(col.dir),
  style({ opacity: 1, gap: 0.4 }),
  palette({ up: "seagreen", down: "indianred" }), y_label("Price"),
  title("Fourteen sessions"))

“Given the candles: x is session, intervals from low to high colored by dir, and also zones from open to close colored by dir.”

Read one session to see the two layers. Session 09 opened at 107.00 and closed at 109.35, so its body is green and runs from 107.00 up to 109.35. Its whisker runs from the session’s low, 106.68, to its high, 109.62. Session 12 closed below where it opened, so its body is red.

color(dir) is written twice, once after each mark. A channel such as color, written after a mark, belongs to that mark alone (scope), so the first colors the whiskers and the second the bodies. Both uses of the column share one legend, because it is one column. Here is the chart with color(dir) after the zone only, beside the chart above:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(candles) + x(session) +
   interval * bounds(low, high) +
   zone * bounds(open, close) +
     color(dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
   palette(c(up = "seagreen", down = "indianred")) +
   y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after the zone only")) |
  (data(candles) + x(session) +
     interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) +
     zone * bounds(open, close) +
       color(dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
     palette(c(up = "seagreen", down = "indianred")) +
     y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after each mark"))
((data(candles) + x(col.session) +
   interval * bounds(col.low, col.high) +
   zone * bounds(col.open, col.close) +
     color(col.dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
   palette({"up": "seagreen", "down": "indianred"}) +
   y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after the zone only")) |
  (data(candles) + x(col.session) +
     interval * bounds(col.low, col.high) + color(col.dir) +
     zone * bounds(col.open, col.close) +
       color(col.dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
     palette({"up": "seagreen", "down": "indianred"}) +
     y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after each mark")))
(data(candles) + x(:session) + interval * bounds(:low, :high) +
  zone * bounds(:open, :close) + color(:dir) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette(["up" => "seagreen", "down" => "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after the zone only")) |
  (data(candles) + x(:session) + interval * bounds(:low, :high) +
  color(:dir) + zone * bounds(:open, :close) + color(:dir) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette(["up" => "seagreen", "down" => "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Price") + title("color(dir) after each mark"))
beside(plot(data(candles), x(col.session),
  layer(interval, bounds(col.low, col.high)),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.open, col.close)), color(col.dir),
  style({ opacity: 1, gap: 0.4 }),
  palette({ up: "seagreen", down: "indianred" }), y_label("Price"),
  title("color(dir) after the zone only")),
  plot(data(candles), x(col.session),
  layer(interval, bounds(col.low, col.high)), color(col.dir),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.open, col.close)), color(col.dir),
  style({ opacity: 1, gap: 0.4 }),
  palette({ up: "seagreen", down: "indianred" }), y_label("Price"),
  title("color(dir) after each mark")))

“Given the candles: x is session, intervals from low to high, and also zones from open to close colored by dir, beside the same with the intervals colored by dir too.”

On the left, no color follows the interval, so every whisker is dark gray, while the bodies are green and red. On the right, each whisker takes its session’s color, as session 12’s red whisker shows.

In palette(), each value of dir is written beside its color, so up is seagreen and down is indianred (Colors by name). Colors written without names are assigned in the order the values of dir first appear. So a table whose first session fell draws down in seagreen. A value written beside its color keeps that color, whatever the order of the rows. Another column name, other values and other colors are written the same way. For a column move with the values rise and fall, write color(move) after each mark and palette(c(rise = "steelblue", fall = "darkorange")).

A table may hold only one of the two values, as in a week when the price fell in every session. On such a table gog refuses the sentence: palette() names “up”, and dir has no category called that. Give dir a declared order that includes both values (Declaring the order of categories). The declared order makes up a category of dir, even though no row holds it. So gog draws each week’s table from the same sentence.

The sessions are the weekdays from Monday, March 2, to Thursday, March 19, 2026. Every chart so far gives each session an equal slot, because session is text. A weekend gets no slot of its own, as on most trading charts. day holds the same sessions as dates, and a date column gets a calendar axis. A CSV file cannot record that a column holds dates, so convert day after reading the table, as A date shows. On a calendar axis, each body takes the smallest distance between two dates as its slot, here one day, as a bar does (Scales). So a weekend stays empty:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(candles) + x(day) +
  interval * bounds(low, high) + color(dir) +
  zone * bounds(open, close) +
    color(dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette(c(up = "seagreen", down = "indianred")) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions on a calendar axis")
(data(candles) + x(col.day) +
  interval * bounds(col.low, col.high) + color(col.dir) +
  zone * bounds(col.open, col.close) +
    color(col.dir) + style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette({"up": "seagreen", "down": "indianred"}) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions on a calendar axis"))
data(candles) + x(:day) + interval * bounds(:low, :high) + color(:dir) +
  zone * bounds(:open, :close) + color(:dir) +
  style(opacity = 1, gap = 0.4) +
  palette(["up" => "seagreen", "down" => "indianred"]) +
  y_label("Price") + title("Fourteen sessions on a calendar axis")
plot(data(candles), x(col.day),
  layer(interval, bounds(col.low, col.high)), color(col.dir),
  layer(zone, bounds(col.open, col.close)), color(col.dir),
  style({ opacity: 1, gap: 0.4 }),
  palette({ up: "seagreen", down: "indianred" }), y_label("Price"),
  title("Fourteen sessions on a calendar axis"))

“Given the candles: x is day, intervals from low to high colored by dir, and also zones from open to close colored by dir.”

The two wide gaps, just before March 9 and March 16, are the weekends. If your table has only dates, convert them to text before the plot to give each session an equal slot.

There is no candlestick atom. The chart is made of atoms that already exist: two marks, the bounds transform, the channels x and color, and the settings style and palette.

19.7 Cells cut from the data: the heatmap

So far every zone has been a rectangle you chose, its sides named by columns you already had. There is a second way to get sides, and it needs no new mark: let bin cut them.

The gm_all table holds every Gapminder year: 142 countries, each measured in 12 years, so 1704 rows. Each row is one country in one year, a country-year. Drawn as points, the crowded middle becomes one dark mass, because a thousand dots in one place look exactly like two hundred. Cut the plane into cells and count the rows in each instead. A plot of cells shaded by their counts is a heatmap. Here are the points beside the cells:

gm_all: first 5 of 1704 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.801 8425333 779.4453
Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.332 9240934 820.8530
Afghanistan Asia 1962 31.997 10267083 853.1007
Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.020 11537966 836.1971
Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.088 13079460 739.9811
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gm_all) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("1704 country-years as points")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("The same rows, counted in cells"))
((data(gm_all) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("1704 country-years as points")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("The same rows, counted in cells")))
(data(gm_all) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("1704 country-years as points")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same rows, counted in cells"))
beside(plot(data(gm_all), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("1704 country-years as points")),
  plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same rows, counted in cells")))

“Given all the gapminder years: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, beside zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

On the left, the upper part of the points, from about $3,000 to $30,000 and 65 to 80 years, is one solid patch of blue. On the right, the same patch is cut into cells. The darkest cell, from about $6,800 to $8,700 and 70 to 73 years, holds 40 country-years. Overlapping points cannot show that number. The dark cells also rise from lower left to upper right. So where GDP per person is higher, life expectancy is usually higher too.

Both plots draw all 12 years together for one reason: to show what a heatmap does with many crowded points. Each country has 12 rows, one for each year, so one cell can hold the same country more than once. The darkest cell’s 40 country-years come from 28 countries, and six of them, such as Bulgaria and Jamaica, are counted more than once. So to compare countries, you usually draw each year separately: a panel for each year, once year is a categorical column (Faceting), or one year alone. But one year has too few rows for cells this small. Drawn alone with bin(24), the 142 rows of 2007 fall in 95 cells, and 66 of those cells hold only one row. For 2007, a plot of the points already shows almost everything those cells show. So this section keeps all 12 years, and its cells hold country-years, not countries.

bin is not the zone’s own transform. The mark decides how many axes bin cuts, and how each count is drawn:

Mark derived by bin Shape
bar * bin one axis cut, with the count in each interval drawn as the height of a histogram’s bar
zone * bin two axes cut, with the count in each cell drawn as that cell’s shade in a heatmap
surface * bin the same two axes, with the count in each cell drawn as the height of a sheet in the cube

The same cells can show their counts as heights instead. Change the mark to bar and add space(), and each cell becomes a separate bar rising in the cube. In the cube a bar measures along the third axis, so bin cuts the other two. The 3-D histogram section draws the heatmap and these bars one after the other and compares what each one shows. surface * bin, the table’s last row, joins the heights into one sheet instead. The surface chapter draws such a sheet from the iris_flowers table.

Three things in the heatmap’s sentence need explaining: bin cut both axes, the count became the color, and you can write that color() yourself.

bin cut both axes, and nothing asked it to. It is the same transform that makes a histogram, and how many axes it cuts is taken from the mark rather than requested. A bar leaves one axis free to measure a height along, so bar * bin cuts the other one. A zone’s cell needs an extent on both axes before it can be a rectangle at all, so zone * bin cuts every axis that has a width to cut, which here is both of them. One transform, one word, readings decided by what the mark needs. There is no separate two-axis bin, like ggplot2’s geom_bin_2d(). The grid of cells a cut makes is called the mesh. Note the words has a width to cut: the mixed mesh is where they matter, because a categorical axis is already cut, and bin does not cut it.

The count became the color, although no color() was written. Both positions were taken, so the measurement went to the one channel left that can carry a number, and the legend is titled Count. This is what bar * bin already does for the y axis: a transform that writes a column also says where it goes.

Color usually tells categories apart. In a plot whose points are colored by continent, Africa’s color does not mean a larger number than Europe’s, or a smaller one. The two colors are only different. In a heatmap, color shows an amount. With the default blues, a darker cell holds more rows, just as a longer bar shows a larger number. The legend shows about how many rows each shade stands for.

A zone’s color takes a continuous column like the count, and gives each value a color from a ramp. bar, area and ribbon take only categories in color. A bar, an area and a ribbon already show a number by their length or by their edges. A heatmap cell does not: bin sets the size and edges of every cell, so only a cell’s color shows its count. That is why a heatmap needs no new mark: its cells are zones, colored by their counts.

The column bin writes is called count, and you can write color(count) yourself. That is not a different plot. It is the same sentence with nothing left implied:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Without color()")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     color(count) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("With color(count)"))
((data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("Without color()")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
     color(col.count) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("With color(count)")))
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Without color()")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:count) + x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("With color(count)"))
beside(plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Without color()")),
  plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.count), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("With color(count)")))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, beside the same with color by count.”

Apart from the titles, the two plots are the same: the same cells, in the same colors, with the same legend.

Writing color(count) gives the colors a place for their options, such as a scale. A channel’s options are set inside its parentheses: x(gdp, scale = "log") puts the x axis on a log scale, and color(count, scale = "log") puts the colors on a log scale too. A sentence without color() has no place to write them.

The counts here are skewed, and a log scale spreads out the small ones. The fullest cell holds 40 country-years, but half of the cells hold 4 or fewer. The default ramp spreads its colors evenly from 1 to 40, so those cells all get almost the same pale blue, and a cell with one row is hard to tell from a cell with four. Here are the same cells on a log ramp:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(count, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  color(col.count, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:count, scale = "log") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), color(col.count, { scale: "log" }),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same cells, counted on a log ramp"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by count on a log scale.”

Now the cells with few rows get distinct shades: a cell with one row is clearly paler than a cell with four. But the cells along the dark diagonal, with 10 to 40 rows, now differ less from each other.

The legend still runs from 1 to 40. A log scale changes which color each count gets, not the counts themselves, just as the x axis on its log scale still shows dollars (1K, 10K, 100K). In the legend, only the middle label changes. On the default ramp the middle color stands for 20.5, halfway between 1 and 40. On the log ramp it stands for 6.32, the geometric mean of 1 and 40: from 1 to 6.32 and from 6.32 to 40, the count is multiplied by the same amount, about 6.3. So the paler half of the ramp goes to the counts from 1 to 6.32.

The empty gaps are cells where no country-year fell. They are left as panel, not painted the pale end of the ramp, because that end stands for a count of one. The uneven edge you get instead is the region the data actually covers, which is information rather than a gap the renderer failed to fill.

bin(24) sets the mesh, the grid of cells the cut makes, exactly as it does on a histogram, and one number cuts both axes into that many bins. A coarser mesh shows less detail, and the plot looks less precise too:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(8) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same data, eight bins a side")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(8)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same data, eight bins a side"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 8, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

Notice that the log scale still applies. bin cuts the log axis into equal steps, so every cell is equally wide on the page. In dollars, though, a cell on the right covers far more than a cell on the left. That suits a variable that runs from a few hundred dollars to a hundred thousand. Most country-years, 77% of them, are under $10,000, and the log axis gives that range more than half of its width.

These cells are solid, although no opacity was set. A zone you place yourself, like the target band at the start of the chapter, is pale by default, so the gridlines and other layers still show through it. A cell that bin cuts gets every side from the data, and its color shows its count. So it is solid by default, and the gridlines under it do not show through. What you can set lists both defaults.

19.8 Hexagons: the other mesh

Does the grid pattern in a heatmap come from the data or from the mesh? The cells drawn so far are rectangles, the default tiling = "rect", and that is a choice rather than a fact about binning. Say tiling = "hex" and the plane is cut a different way. The two plots below differ only in tiling:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   palette("viridis") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("tiling = \"rect\", the default")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") +
     y(life) + palette("viridis") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("tiling = \"hex\""))
((data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
   palette("viridis") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
   title("tiling = \"rect\", the default")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
     y(col.life) + palette("viridis") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
     title("tiling = \"hex\"")))
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  palette("viridis") + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("tiling = \"rect\", the default")) |
  (data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") +
  x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + palette("viridis") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("tiling = \"hex\""))
beside(plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20)),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), palette("viridis"),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("tiling = \"rect\", the default")),
  plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20, { tiling: "hex" })),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), palette("viridis"),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("tiling = \"hex\"")))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette, beside zones derived by bin into 20 on hexagons, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette.”

Both plots also change two things from the first heatmap. bin(20) cuts a little coarser than its bin(24), and palette("viridis") replaces the default ramp of blues. Viridis suits a count. It is built so that equal steps in the number look like equal steps in brightness. It runs from dark purple for the fewest rows to bright yellow for the most, the reverse of the blues, where darker means more. It changes in hue as well as in lightness, so cells with close counts are easier to distinguish. The palette is a free choice on either mesh, though, so do not read it as something hexagons require.

The hexagonal mesh is chosen for a reason, not for its looks: the rectangular mesh has a defect. A rectangular grid lines up its cell centers in rows and columns, and the eye is very good at seeing rows and columns. So the eye sees that alignment as a pattern in the data, even though the mesh made it. Wilkinson states it directly: rectangular bins “lead the eye to align bin centers and to see regularity where there is none” (Wilkinson, 2005). This defect is one reason Carr and colleagues devised hexagon binning in 1987 (Carr et al., 1987). A hexagonal mesh shifts every second row by half a cell, so each cell is placed between two cells of the next row. The borders between cells zigzag instead of running in long straight lines.

Look along the sparse edges of the two plots. The rectangular cells line up in straight rows and columns, so the edge of the data is made of horizontal and vertical pieces. The hexagons do not line up in columns, and their borders zigzag, so the edge has no long straight pieces and follows the shape of the data more closely.

Each mesh has its use. A rectangle’s sides run parallel to the axes, so each cell’s range on x and on y can be read directly from the axes. Hexagons lose that reading, but their borders zigzag, so the mesh draws no long straight lines of its own. That suits two continuous axes. When an axis is a category, its slots have an order but no distance, so its cells are always rectangles. tiling = "hex" is refused there (What it refuses).

These two are the only meshes gog draws. Copies of only three regular polygons cover a plane with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. Regular octagons, for example, leave square gaps between them. Wilkinson’s grammar lists a triangle mesh too (Wilkinson, 2005), but a triangle mesh adds nothing that rectangles and hexagons lack, so gog leaves it out.

19.8.1 Cells and the shape of the panel

The cells in the heatmaps so far are not squares. In a single plot they are a little wide, and in each plot of a side-by-side pair they are tall. The panel causes this. The cells gog draws are squares and hexagons, stretched by the panel: a number given to bin cuts both axes into that many equal steps on the page, so each cell has the panel’s proportions. theme(ratio = 1) makes the panel square, and then the cells are squares:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  theme(ratio = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Square cells on a square panel")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  theme(ratio = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Square cells on a square panel"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  theme(ratio = 1) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Square cells on a square panel")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), theme({ ratio: 1 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Square cells on a square panel"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with a square panel.”

The hexagons follow the same rule. Each plot of the pair in Hexagons: the other mesh has a tall panel, so its hexagons are stretched upward: their four slanted sides are shorter than their two upright ones. R’s hexbin package lets you set this stretch with its shape argument. In gog the panel sets it, so a square panel removes it. Here is that pair’s hexagon plot again, on a square panel:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") + theme(ratio = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Hexagonal cells on a square panel")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  palette("viridis") + theme(ratio = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Hexagonal cells on a square panel"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + palette("viridis") + theme(ratio = 1) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Hexagonal cells on a square panel")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20, { tiling: "hex" })),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), palette("viridis"),
  theme({ ratio: 1 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Hexagonal cells on a square panel"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 on hexagons, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette, with a square panel.”

Now each hexagon’s six sides are the same length.

19.8.2 Why the mesh belongs to bin

In the rest of this book, a transform computes and the mark decides how the result is drawn. bar * bin, line * bin and step * bin are one histogram drawn three ways. So it would be reasonable to expect the hexagon to be a mark, or a setting on one. It is neither, because hexagons change the numbers the plot draws, not only how the plot looks.

Those three marks all receive the same numbers. A hexagonal mesh shifts every second row of cells by half a cell, which changes which cell each observation falls in, so the counts themselves differ. You cannot draw a hexagonal plot from data binned into rectangles, whatever the mark does with it. The mesh is decided before anything is drawn, so it belongs to the transform that does the cutting.

That is also how Wilkinson organizes it. His bin is not one method but a family of ways to partition a plane, with rect and hex among the members, the two that gog’s tiling takes. The mesh both shapes the cells and tags each row with the cell it fell in. One operation, both effects.

One consequence follows for the other marks: a tiling means nothing to a bin that cuts one axis, because there the cells are intervals and an interval has no shape. So gog refuses bar * bin(tiling = "hex"), and the message names zone as the mark a tiling belongs to:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(life)
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(col.life)
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin({ tiling: "hex" })), x(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `bin(tiling = )` says how to divide a *plane*, and a `bar` bins one axis — its cells are intervals, and an interval has no shape. Drop the tiling for a histogram, or use `zone * bin(tiling = "hex")` to cut both axes into cells and color each by its count.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

19.9 Cells the data estimated: zone * density

Both meshes so far have counted the rows that fell in each cell. A count is exact, but when the table is small, neighboring cells hold very different counts. The iris_flowers table holds 150 iris flowers, each with three measurements and its species.

bin counts the rows in each cell. There is a second thing worth measuring at a cell, and it needs no new mark either: how dense the points are there. That is density, the transform that gives a line its smooth curve. As with bin, a zone’s cell needs an extent on both axes, so gog estimates the density across both. The result is a field, a density estimated at every point of the plane. The zone paints the field, and path traces the same field as contours.

iris_flowers: first 5 of 150 rows
sepal_length sepal_width petal_length species
5.1 3.5 1.4 setosa
4.9 3.0 1.4 setosa
4.7 3.2 1.3 setosa
4.6 3.1 1.5 setosa
5.0 3.6 1.4 setosa

Here the 150 flowers are counted on the 24 × 24 mesh used above, beside the density estimated from the same rows:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * bin(24) + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
   title("zone * bin(24): counted")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) +
     title("zone * density: estimated"))
((data(iris_flowers) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) +
   title("zone * bin(24): counted")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) +
     title("zone * density: estimated")))
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * bin(24) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + title("zone * bin(24): counted")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + title("zone * density: estimated"))
beside(plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.sepal_length),
  y(col.petal_length), title("zone * bin(24): counted")),
  plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density), x(col.sepal_length),
  y(col.petal_length), title("zone * density: estimated")))

“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by bin into 24, x is sepal length, y is petal length, beside zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length.”

Most of what the heatmap showed is true here too. The field was computed across both axes without being asked, the measurement went to color, and color(density) names it out loud and draws the identical plot. zone * bin and zone * density are one plot measured two ways, counted and estimated.

One difference is easy to see. On the left, most of the cells are empty and the fullest holds 6 flowers, so the two clusters break into scattered cells. On the right, there are no empty cells, and each cluster is one smooth patch. A count of zero says no row fell in that cell, so bin leaves it unpainted. An estimate exists at every point of the plane, so the estimator returns a value for every cell and the mesh is painted edge to edge. What it paints is a real density rather than an arbitrary color value. The cell values times the cell areas sum to 1, just as the area under a density curve is 1.

palette() chooses the ramp, exactly as it does for a binned heatmap. As with a count, viridis makes close densities easier to distinguish, because it changes in hue as well as in lightness:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density, viridis")
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density, viridis"))
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") + title("Filled density, viridis")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density), x(col.sepal_length),
  y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("Filled density, viridis"))

“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette.”

One parameter of a painted field is adjust. To estimate a density, density places a small bell-shaped curve on each row and adds the curves up. The width of each curve is the bandwidth, which gog computes from the data, and adjust multiplies that width. It is a multiplier rather than a width in either column’s units, which is why it means the same thing on both axes:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(adjust = 1.6) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same flowers, smoothed more")
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(adjust = 1.6) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same flowers, smoothed more"))
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(adjust = 1.6) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same flowers, smoothed more")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density({ adjust: 1.6 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("The same flowers, smoothed more"))

“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density adjusted by 1.6, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette.”

Compare it with the plot above. The two clusters are wider and blurrier, and the space between them is no longer dark. The highest density in the legend falls from 0.163 to 0.101, because each flower’s curve is spread wider.

The second parameter is places: how many places along each axis the field is computed at. The default is 64 on each axis. The places are the corners of the cells, so 64 places make 63 × 63 cells. Fewer places draw larger cells and a smaller file:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(places = 24) +
   x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
   title("density(places = 24)")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
     x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
     title("density, 64 places"))
((data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(places = 24) +
   x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
   title("density(places = 24)")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density +
     x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
     title("density, 64 places")))
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(places = 24) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") + title("density(places = 24)")) |
  (data(iris_flowers) + zone * density + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") + title("density, 64 places"))
beside(plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density({ places: 24 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("density(places = 24)")),
  plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density), x(col.sepal_length),
  y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"), title("density, 64 places")))

“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density at 24 places, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette, beside zones derived by density, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette.”

The left heatmap has 23 × 23 cells, and its file is about 77 KB. The right one has 63 × 63 cells and is about 545 KB. The file grows with the square of places: about 2.2 MB at 128 places, and about 9 MB at 256, the most places a field allows. So raise places only when the cells are too coarse to read. How many places lists the default of every reading of density.

The same field traced rather than painted is path * density, the contour. The difference between them is the one between bar * bin and line * bin: the mark chooses the shape, and the transform stays the same.

19.10 Bands the data cut: zone * density(levels = )

A smooth ramp is hard to read a value from: two nearby cells differ by a shade too small for the eye to see. Cut the field into a few steps and each band has a level a reader can point to. Ask for levels and the field stops being continuous. It is cut into that many steps, and a zone fills between them:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density bands")
(data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("Filled density bands"))
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(levels = 8) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") + title("Filled density bands")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(zone, density({ levels: 8 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("Filled density bands"))

“Given the iris flowers: zones derived by density at 8 levels, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette.”

That is the filled contour, and levels is the same parameter path takes. levels means one thing, cut the field into this many steps, and each mark then draws that cut its own way: a path traces the boundaries, a zone fills between them. So the two are not two features but one transform read by two marks, and a band’s edge falls exactly on the contour line:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced")
(data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) +
  x(col.sepal_length) + y(col.petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced"))
data(iris_flowers) + path * density(levels = 8) + x(:sepal_length) +
  y(:petal_length) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The same eight levels, traced")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(path, density({ levels: 8 })),
  x(col.sepal_length), y(col.petal_length), palette("viridis"),
  title("The same eight levels, traced"))

“Given the iris flowers: paths derived by density at 8 levels, x is sepal length, y is petal length, with the viridis palette.”

That makes three readings of one transform: line * density is a curve, zone * density a painted field, and path * density a contour.

The bands lie one inside another. A denser region usually lies inside a less dense one, so gog paints the outermost band first and each inner band over it. A band can also have a hole. When points lie around a circle, the density in the middle is low, so each band has a hole there. gog cuts the hole out of the band, and the middle stays unpainted.

19.11 Cells the axes already made: the tile plot

So far the sides have been made in three ways: bounds named them, bin cut them, and density estimated them. The schedule also used a fourth way, on its categorical y axis. Each zone’s top and bottom came from its task’s slot, so no column held them.

The six_weeks table holds six weeks of daily orders, one row per day. Each day has a week and a weekday, so the 42 counts already form a grid: weeks across, weekdays down. The grid itself is the picture you want, and two categorical axes already divide the panel into its cells. The rows begin on a Friday, so the book declares the order of both columns (A declared order). weekday runs from Mon to Sun, and week from Week 1 to Week 6.

A categorical axis is already divided. Six weeks on the x axis is six slots. “Week 3” owns one of those slots, a place on the panel with a left edge and a right edge, and the axis fixes both when it lays out the categories. So a category bounds its own axis, and two categorical positions bound a zone completely, with no transform in the sentence:

six_weeks: first 5 of 42 rows
day orders weekday week
2024-03-01 20 Fri Week 1
2024-03-02 23 Sat Week 1
2024-03-03 25 Sun Week 1
2024-03-04 28 Mon Week 1
2024-03-05 30 Tue Week 1
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(six_weeks) + zone + x(week) + y(weekday) + color(orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time")
(data(six_weeks) + zone + x(col.week) + y(col.weekday) + color(col.orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time"))
data(six_weeks) + zone + x(:week) + y(:weekday) + color(:orders) +
  title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time")
plot(data(six_weeks), zone, x(col.week), y(col.weekday),
  color(col.orders), title("Six weeks of orders, a day at a time"))

“Given the six weeks table: zones, x is week, y is weekday, color by orders.”

That is a tile plot, here in the form called a calendar heatmap, and the whole of it is zone + x + y + color. What makes it worth drawing is that 42 daily counts carry two patterns at once, one by week and one by weekday. A list of numbers shows neither, while a grid separates them by direction. Compare the columns to see the weeks: week four is the palest, the lowest week. Compare the rows to see the weekdays: the Thursday row is the darkest overall, and the Friday row the palest. The extremes are the cells where the two patterns agree: the darkest cell is Thursday of week six, and the palest are the Friday and Saturday of week four.

The rule behind the tile plot is short: a category owns a slot, a number is a point. A point has no width, so two continuous positions leave a zone with nothing to bound it until a transform such as bin gives it sides. The tile plot needed nothing new: no mark, no transform and no channel was added to the kernel.

19.11.1 bin cuts, count tallies

The six_weeks table has one row per cell already. Often a table does not: you hold the raw observations and want to know how many fell in each cell. The winds table is one of these. Each row is one observation of the wind. direction is where it blew from, one of eight compass points, and bearing is the same direction in degrees. Each row also holds the wind’s speed and the season. The transform that tallies the rows in each cell is count, exactly as it is for a bar chart:

winds: first 5 of 264 rows
direction bearing speed season
N 19.612260 10.1 Winter
N 357.049499 11.0 Winter
N 349.709737 13.8 Winter
N 2.602499 7.4 Winter
N 338.210715 3.7 Summer
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + zone * count + x(direction) + y(season) +
  title("Wind observations by direction and season")
(data(winds) + zone * count + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) +
  title("Wind observations by direction and season"))
data(winds) + zone * count + x(:direction) + y(:season) +
  title("Wind observations by direction and season")
plot(data(winds), layer(zone, count), x(col.direction), y(col.season),
  title("Wind observations by direction and season"))

“Given the winds: zones derived by count, x is direction, y is season.”

That is the shape of a confusion matrix, the table that counts predicted classes against actual ones. A confusion matrix is the same sentence with different columns. The iris_predicted table holds the 150 iris flowers, each with its species, actual, and a species predicted from petal length alone: below 2.5 cm setosa, below 4.8 cm versicolor, otherwise virginica. That rule was made for this example; no model was fitted:

iris_predicted: first 5 of 150 rows
actual predicted
setosa setosa
setosa setosa
setosa setosa
setosa setosa
setosa setosa
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_predicted) + zone * count + x(actual) + y(predicted) +
  palette("viridis") + title("Species predicted from petal length alone")
(data(iris_predicted) + zone * count + x(col.actual) + y(col.predicted) +
  palette("viridis") + title("Species predicted from petal length alone"))
data(iris_predicted) + zone * count + x(:actual) + y(:predicted) +
  palette("viridis") + title("Species predicted from petal length alone")
plot(data(iris_predicted), layer(zone, count), x(col.actual),
  y(col.predicted), palette("viridis"),
  title("Species predicted from petal length alone"))

“Given the iris predicted table: zones derived by count, x is actual, y is predicted, with the viridis palette.”

The bright cells on the diagonal are the flowers predicted correctly: all 50 setosa, 44 versicolor and 49 virginica. Off the diagonal, 6 versicolor were predicted as virginica and 1 virginica as versicolor. The other cells hold no flower, so they are left empty.

Notice what was not needed there. bin cuts a continuous axis into cells before anything can be counted in them; a categorical axis is already cut, so there is nothing left to do but tally. bar * bin and bar * count follow the same rule on one axis; here both axes follow it. So each refusal names the other transform: give zone * count a continuous axis and it names bin, and give zone * bin two categorical axes and it names count.

A tile plot has two categorical positions where a bar chart has one. That second position changes only where the tally is written. A bar has a length to put it on, so bar * count writes its tally to the y axis. A tile plot’s two positions are both taken by categories, so zone * count writes its tally to color, and the legend is titled Count.

proportion is the same tally as a share of the whole, which is the plot to draw when the absolute numbers are not what you want to read:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + zone * proportion + x(direction) + y(season) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares")
(data(winds) + zone * proportion + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares"))
data(winds) + zone * proportion + x(:direction) + y(:season) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The same observations, as shares")
plot(data(winds), layer(zone, proportion), x(col.direction),
  y(col.season), palette("viridis"),
  title("The same observations, as shares"))

“Given the winds: zones derived by proportion, x is direction, y is season.”

That share is of every row counted, not of a row or a column of the grid. A confusion matrix divided by the total of each actual class needs a different denominator. proportion always divides by the whole table, so compute each class’s shares in R, Python, Julia or JavaScript and draw them as a tile plot.

proportion reads a cut mesh the same way. Compose it with bin and the heatmap’s counts become shares of the whole, the relative-frequency histogram with a second axis. The plot reads the gm_all table, shown in Cells cut from the data: the heatmap:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  palette("viridis") + title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) * proportion + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + palette("viridis") +
  title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20), proportion),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), palette("viridis"),
  title("The heatmap, as shares of all 1704 rows"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 and proportion, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, with the viridis palette.”

proportion leaves the cells exactly where bin cut them, and the legend now reads in shares. The legend’s top value, 0.0264, is the share in the fullest cell: 45 of the 1704 rows.

19.11.2 count tallies rows, mean reduces a column

The wind table records more than which cell each observation fell in. Each row also carries a speed, and the question “how fast, on average, in each cell?” is not a tally at all; it is a summary of one column.

The first sentence to try is a plain tile plot, and it is refused. A zone draws one opaque rectangle for each row, and here many rows share each cell. Their rectangles would be drawn one on top of another, so each cell would show only the color of its last row. gog counts the rows that would be hidden, and names the summary to write instead:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + zone + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)
data(winds) + zone + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) + color(col.speed)
data(winds) + zone + x(:direction) + y(:season) + color(:speed)
plot(data(winds), zone, x(col.direction), y(col.season), color(col.speed))
Error:
! gog: a `zone` draws one opaque rectangle per row, and 16 of its 16 cells hold rows with different `color(speed)`, so each of those cells would show only its last row, and 248 rows would be hidden. For one value per cell, summarize the rows: `zone * mean + color(speed)` draws each cell's mean, and `median`, `sum`, `max` and `min` do the same.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

zone * mean draws one rectangle for each cell, colored by the mean speed of its rows:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed) +
  title("Mean wind speed, by direction and season")
(data(winds) + zone * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) + color(col.speed) +
  title("Mean wind speed, by direction and season"))
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(:direction) + y(:season) + color(:speed) +
  title("Mean wind speed, by direction and season")
plot(data(winds), layer(zone, mean), x(col.direction), y(col.season),
  color(col.speed), title("Mean wind speed, by direction and season"))

“Given the winds: zones derived by mean, x is direction, y is season, color by speed.”

Compare that with zone * count in the section above. The sentence has the same shape, with mean for count and one more binding. count was handed no column, so it counts rows and writes a new column, count. mean was handed one, and color(speed) says which column it reduced. All six summaries read a mesh this way (sum, mean, median, max, min and quantile), and each writes its answer back into the column it reduced.

Because the answer is written back into that column, you name the column on the channel that carries the measurement. On a bar chart, that channel is the continuous axis. In bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life), it is y: y(life) names the column, and each bar’s height is the mean of life for its continent. On a zone, both positions are taken, so the measurement goes to color, as the heatmap showed. In the sentence above, color(speed) names the column, and each cell’s color is the mean of speed for its direction and season.

The whole rule is short. A summary reduces the column on the channel that carries the measurement, and it groups by every position that does not carry the measurement. So bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) groups by x. With horizontal bars, bar * mean + x(life) + y(continent) groups by y. A zone measures with color, so it groups by both positions. In the cube a bar measures with z, so it also groups by both of the other positions. A summary also groups by any channel that splits the rows into groups. bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) draws one mean for each pair of continent and era, side by side.

A summary composes with proportion too: each cell’s summary becomes a share of the total over all cells. The titanic table already holds counts: each row is a group of people aboard, and n is the size of the group. So sum adds up the people in each cell, and proportion turns each sum into a share of everyone aboard. Counting rows would not answer the question here: zone * proportion gives every cell 0.125, because each cell holds 4 of the table’s 32 rows.

titanic: first 5 of 32 rows
class sex age survived n
1st Male Adult Yes 57
1st Male Adult No 118
1st Male Child Yes 5
1st Male Child No 0
1st Female Adult Yes 140
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(titanic) + zone * sum * proportion + x(class) + y(survived) + color(n) +
  title("Everyone aboard, as shares: class by survival")
(data(titanic) + zone * sum * proportion + x(col["class"]) + y(col.survived) + color(col.n) +
  title("Everyone aboard, as shares: class by survival"))
data(titanic) + zone * sum * proportion + x(:class) + y(:survived) +
  color(:n) + title("Everyone aboard, as shares: class by survival")
plot(data(titanic), layer(zone, sum, proportion), x(col.class),
  y(col.survived), color(col.n),
  title("Everyone aboard, as shares: class by survival"))

“Given titanic: zones derived by sum and proportion, x is class, y is survived, color by n.”

The legend is titled Proportion, because its numbers are now shares of everyone aboard. color(n) still names the column that sum adds up. The darkest cell holds the crew who did not survive: 0.306, about three in ten of everyone aboard. Space draws the same table as bars in the cube, with bar * sum and z(n). There the angle has to be chosen so that no bar hides another, while this tile plot shows all eight groups at once.

Say mean with nothing for it to reduce and the engine asks for the column rather than guessing, as What it refuses shows.

A summary also needs cells to summarize into. The six summaries measure without cutting, so each axis must already be divided. What it refuses shows the refusal and the two ways to fix the sentence.

19.11.3 Cells cut, then summarized: the summary heatmap

The last two sections let the axes supply the cells. This section and the next put bin back in the sentence. How does life expectancy depend on income and on time together? Both are continuous, so neither axis is divided into cells yet. bin cuts them, and mean measures inside each:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) * mean + x(year) + y(gdp, scale = "log") +
  color(life) + title("Mean life expectancy, by era and income")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) * mean + x(col.year) + y(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
  color(col.life) + title("Mean life expectancy, by era and income"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) * mean + x(:year) + y(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  color(:life) + title("Mean life expectancy, by era and income")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(12), mean), x(col.year),
  y(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), color(col.life),
  title("Mean life expectancy, by era and income"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 12 and mean, x is year, y is gdp on a log scale, color by life.”

bin(12) cuts the plane into cells, mean reduces life inside each, and color both names that column and carries the answer, exactly as it does on the tile plot above. Read the panel from bottom left to top right and you can see both patterns. Life expectancy rises with income up the panel, and rises again with time across it.

year is continuous, but the table holds only every fifth year, from 1952 to 2007. For evenly spaced values like these, choose the number of bins so that every bin holds the same number of them. With bin(15), there are fifteen columns of cells for twelve years, so three columns hold no year and stay empty. Twelve bins put exactly one of the table’s years in each column of cells.

bin(12) cuts the same cells with or without mean. What changes is the color: with mean, it no longer shows how many rows fell in each cell. Without mean, the same cells are counted:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) + x(year) + y(gdp, scale = "log") +
  title("The same cells, counted")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) + x(col.year) + y(col.gdp, scale = "log") +
  title("The same cells, counted"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(12) + x(:year) + y(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  title("The same cells, counted")
